claim: ~81% of cross-cultural narrative pairings share only one exact motif, so context-free motif atoms barely align across traditions
evidence: Machine-readable Motif-Index case study on a 1,969-narrative South American subset
limit: One regional subset; finding applied by analogy and not measured on the Atlas corpus

claim: Motif tagging by a single team exhibits encoder bias, so the tagging scheme itself must be exposed as interpretive
evidence: "The entire motif mapping was done by the same team and therefore exhibits encoder bias"; "Not many things in scholarship are as treacherous as a bad classification"
limit: Writes about their own project; it motivates but does not prove the Atlas's design

claim: The 270-tag motif layer is deliberately coarse (28 cross-tradition families) and borrows Thompson/ATU codes where they exist
evidence: src/data/motifs.json records Thompson codes; student journal weighs what borrowing preserves (searchability) against what it hides (emic meaning)
limit: Code reuse aids search but imports Thompson's Western ordering of motifs

claim: Map pins for myth places are interpretive claims rather than data points
evidence: Crampton and Krygier: "maps make reality as much as they represent it"; the Atlas Map subtitle states the same to its users
locator: Crampton and Krygier 2005 p. 15; Map view UI
limit: The scholarly claim is documented; the subtitle wording is the design's own

claim: Symbolic or otherworldly places receive a neutral inland coordinate plus an explanatory note
evidence: Corpus template field rule "note how you chose it" and student placement questions (disputed territories; shared myths; shifting borders)
limit: A design convention; no historical source prescribes a coordinate rule

claim: Re-enacted personas raise engagement and emotional connection but lower knowledge delivery, so an objective voice must remain available
evidence: Museum study comparing a re-enacted King chatbot with a docent
limit: One museum study in Korea; generalising it to 153 fictional figures is the Atlas's inference

claim: Persona framing does not improve answer accuracy, so the chat's honest claims are engagement and interpretation only
evidence: Across 4 LLM families and 162 personas, no statistically significant accuracy gain over control
limit: Objective MMLU tasks and open-weight models only; does not measure role-play engagement

claim: Scholarly chat mode cites only real corpus passages with confidence while dramatic mode is banner-labelled fictional
evidence: src/lib/mockChat.js mode split; plan red line "the chatbot is always labelled fictional"
limit: The split is a design invention responding to the two documented findings above; citations are only as good as the public-domain corpus

claim: Traditions where myth and religion share one origin receive a myth-religion category instead of a forced split
evidence: category field documentation naming Hindu / Norse / Yoruba / Afro-Atlantic / Celtic
limit: Interpretive division; reasoning is noted in the data where ambiguous

claim: Search bridges singular and plural stems and Greek/Roman name equivalences so queries find the same stories
evidence: Playtest found "apple/appl" split and Hercules vs Heracles misses; stemmer fixed and name-equivalence table added, each with regression tests
limit: The equivalence table covers common pairs only

claim: The chat roster passes the same curatorial policy as the corpus, so restricted traditions stay excluded everywhere
evidence: Six figures from excluded traditions leaked into the picker; roster now policy-filtered with a unit test
limit: The exclusion policy itself is the design's own curatorial decision

claim: Corpus frozen at 5494 texts / 39 traditions / 270 motifs with source URL / license / mandatory sensitivity flag per text; restricted traditions fail validation
evidence: docs/plan.md scope and boundaries plus scripts/01_build_corpus.py validation
limit: Public-domain translations only; corpus gaps are logged in questions.md (e.g. no Adam and Eve text)
